ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging in Chicago, IL
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection on Chicago refinery, steel, rail and bridge equipment, mobilized to your site. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Chicago, Illinois
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic testing technicians to Chicago plants, mills, rail yards and fabrication shops for wall-thickness surveys, corrosion checks and shear-wave examination of welds. Send us the equipment list, the code you work to and the access conditions, and we will scope the job around them. Request a UT quote for your Chicago site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Chicago

Chicago sits where Lake Michigan meets the busiest rail interchange in North America, and that mix drives the UT work around the city. On the Indiana lakeshore, minutes from the Illinois line, the Whiting refinery processes more than 400,000 barrels of crude a day, and refineries at Joliet and Lemont sit southwest of the city along the Des Plaines and Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal corridor. Process piping, columns, drums and exchangers at plants like these lose wall slowly through corrosion and erosion, and ultrasonic thickness readings are how an owner tracks that loss from one campaign to the next.

Away from the refineries, the same instrument is used on a very different mix of steel. Integrated mills along the southern lakeshore run furnace shells, gas mains, cooling circuits and crane rails. Rail shops and bridge owners deal with fatigue-prone steel that has been in service for decades. Chicago also has 37 movable bridges inside the city limits, mostly the trunnion bascule design, and each of them carries steel girders, floor beams and machinery supports that need periodic examination. Warehouses, distribution centers and commercial towers add structural steel and crane runways to the list.

  • Refinery and chemical plant piping, vessels and tanks: wall thickness at condition monitoring locations
  • Steel mill structures, ladle and crane components, and gas piping: thickness and weld checks
  • Bridge and rail steel: plate thickness at corroded bearing and splash areas, weld examination at repairs
  • Fabrication shops: plate lamination checks and production weld examination

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends a short sound pulse into the metal and times the echo. For a thickness job that echo comes from the back wall, so the instrument reports the remaining wall directly. For a weld job it comes from reflectors inside the weld: lack of fusion, cracks, slag lines and porosity that sit below the surface where visual and surface methods cannot see them. That is why UT is the usual volumetric method when a code allows it and radiography is not practical.

It has limits that matter on Chicago steel. Sound needs a smooth enough surface and a liquid couplant, so heavy scale, flaking paint and rough weld caps have to be dressed first. Pitted walls scatter the beam and can make a thickness reading jump, which is why the technician watches the A-scan trace rather than trusting a bare number. Coarse-grained castings and some cladding attenuate sound badly. And a thickness reading describes the spot under the probe, not the ten square feet around it, so the spacing of the readings is part of the procedure. When the question is a surface-breaking crack on a ferromagnetic part, magnetic particle or penetrant testing answers it better, and we say so rather than sell UT where it does not fit.

Codes, acceptance criteria and Illinois rules

For most Chicago refinery and plant work the governing documents are the owner's inspection program and the construction code. ASME Section V Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds and Article 5 covers materials, while ASTM E797 governs contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. Acceptance of weld indications comes from the code that built the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and AWS D1.5 where the owner is a bridge authority. In-service equipment follows API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. In each case the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and reports the data that inspector needs.

Illinois adds its own layer. The Division of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety at the Office of the State Fire Marshal requires internal inspection of high pressure boilers every year, low pressure boilers every two years and pressure vessels every three years, and it does not allow non-code boilers or pressure vessels to be installed. Inside the city limits the City of Chicago Boiler Inspection Bureau, part of the Department of Buildings, inspects boilers and unfired pressure vessels itself. Thickness data on a registered vessel often ends up in front of one of those inspectors, so readings are recorded against fixed locations they can find again. The state and city pages are worth reading before you plan a campaign: Illinois boiler and pressure vessel FAQs and the Chicago boiler inspection page. Across the border in Indiana the state's own boiler program applies, so a Whiting-area job follows Indiana rules rather than Illinois ones. Process safety management under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) adds the requirement that inspection follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, which is how most owners justify a written thickness program.

How thickness gauging is done

Corroded steel is gauged with a dual-element probe, which separates transmit and receive crystals so the instrument can read pitted or thin wall that a single-element probe would misjudge. The technician calibrates on a step block made of the same material as the part, checks the zero and velocity, and verifies the setup again at the end of the shift. With an A-scan display the pulse shape is visible, so a doubled echo on thin wall or a laminar reflection can be spotted and rejected instead of logged as a false reading.

The readings go on a grid that matches your isometric or vessel drawing. Each condition monitoring location gets a permanent mark, and the same point is read every campaign, which turns a pile of numbers into a corrosion rate. Hot lines need high-temperature probes, a couplant rated for the surface, and a correction for the temperature of the wall, because sound travels more slowly in hot steel and an uncorrected reading comes out thick. Insulated lines mean someone has to open a window in the jacketing, and that request belongs in the plan before the crew arrives.

Shear-wave examination of welds

Weld examination uses an angle-beam probe, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees, that sends shear waves through the weld volume from the side of the joint. The technician builds a reference level, often a distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block of matching thickness, then scans from both sides where access allows and evaluates each indication by amplitude, length and position. Planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks reflect strongly when the beam meets them squarely, which is why the scan plan and the weld geometry have to be worked out together.

The procedure, not the technician's judgment on the day, sets what is recorded and what is rejected. We write it to the governing code, an ASNT Level III approves it, and the indication log shows the reference level used so a second examiner could repeat the work. On a Chicago bridge repair or a mill structure, where the weld may be thick and the access awkward, that written scan plan is also what lets the owner's engineer accept the result.

Who does the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up and calibrates the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports; the Level III behind our UT work is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Chicago. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so the crew you get is assembled for your job rather than pulled from a local pool, and we confirm travel and site orientation requirements when we quote. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your contract needs a specific scheme or a customer-specific qualification, tell us at the start so we can confirm what is realistic.

What the UT report contains

A useful ultrasonic report lets someone repeat the job. Ours identifies the component and its location, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and surface condition, and the technician's name and level. Thickness work includes the grid with every reading, the nominal and minimum required thickness where you supply them, and flags for readings below the limit. Weld work includes a sketch showing each indication with position, length and amplitude against the reference level, plus an accept or reject call against the acceptance criteria you named. An ASNT Level III reviews the report before it goes to you. If your inspector needs the data in a particular layout for an API 510 or API 570 program, say so when you request the quote.

Planning a UT job in Chicago

Weather and access shape most Chicago jobs. Winter work outdoors means cold steel, frozen couplant and gloved hands trying to hold a probe steady; couplant rated for low temperature and a warm-up plan for the instrument save time. Lake wind off the water makes scaffold and ladder work harder on the lakeshore sites. Summer brings heat and humidity that affect both people and hot-surface readings. Refinery and mill outages are scheduled well in advance, so the right time to talk is before the work scope is frozen, not after the shutdown starts. Plants in the Calumet region and the Joliet corridor run badge and safety orientation processes that take time to clear, and Chicago bridge and rail work often requires track or lane access that has to be booked through the owner. Tell us about those steps early and we will build them into the schedule instead of discovering them at the gate.

UT, MT or PT for your Chicago job

Choose the method by the question you are asking. If it is how much wall is left on a pipe or tank shell, or whether a weld has internal flaws, ultrasonic testing is the tool. If you need to find a surface crack at a fillet weld or a lifting lug on carbon steel, magnetic particle testing in Chicago is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the part is stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic material, penetrant testing in Chicago is the way to find open cracks. Many scopes use two methods together, for example UT for thickness and MT on the repair welds. Our national ultrasonic testing page explains the service in general terms, and the ultrasonic testing guide goes deeper on the physics. For standards detail, see the explainer on ultrasonic thickness measurement requirements.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Some Chicago employers would rather build their own bench than hire it in. Atlantis trains technicians in ultrasonic testing through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, delivered as online theory with a practical examination at your facility, and your own written practice defines what qualifies a person under SNT-TC-1A. The Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator gives trainees scanning practice before they touch real steel. If you are setting up a group, read about NDT training in Chicago, check SNT-TC-1A eligibility and try the practice tests. For a written practice or Level III oversight, see outsourced Level III consulting. Statewide coverage is on our Illinois inspection services page.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Chicago?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Chicago. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so the quote includes the travel and site orientation your plant requires. We confirm those details before work starts.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing measure on a Chicago refinery pipe or vessel?
faq.a: Remaining wall thickness at marked condition monitoring locations, plus internal flaws in welds. Readings are repeated at the same points each campaign so your inspector can calculate a corrosion rate and set the next interval.

faq.q: Can UT find surface cracks?
faq.a: Sometimes, but it is not the first choice. A surface crack on carbon steel is usually found faster with magnetic particle testing, and on stainless or aluminum with penetrant testing. We recommend the method that answers your question.

faq.q: Which codes do you examine to?
faq.a: The one governing your item: ASME Section V Articles 4 and 5 for technique, ASTM E797 for thickness, and the acceptance rules of Section VIII, B31.3, AWS D1.1 or D1.5. The owner or engineer names the code before work starts.

faq.q: Do you perform API 510, 570 or 653 inspections?
faq.a: No. Under those codes your authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and gives that inspector the thickness and indication data in a form they can use.

faq.q: Do Chicago boilers and pressure vessels have special rules?
faq.a: Yes. Illinois sets inspection cycles through the State Fire Marshal, and inside the city limits the Chicago Boiler Inspection Bureau inspects boilers and unfired pressure vessels. We record readings against fixed locations so those inspectors can use the data.

faq.q: What do I need to send for a quote?
faq.a: The equipment list or drawings, the code or specification, the material and approximate thickness, the surface and insulation condition, the dates of any outage, and any site badging steps. The more detail you send, the tighter the scope.

faq.q: Who certifies your technicians?
faq.a: Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which is how the employer certifies its own personnel. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports, and we can show the qualification record on request.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Chicago, IL | MT Testing
mt.description: Mag particle testing (MPI) of welds, lifting gear, rail components and plant steel in Chicago, with wet fluorescent and yoke methods. Ask for a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Chicago, Illinois
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends magnetic particle technicians to Chicago-area refineries, mills, rail shops and fabricators to find surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Typical jobs are repair and attachment welds, crane hooks and lifting lugs, axle and wheel components, and structural joints. Request an MT quote for your Chicago site with the part list and code, and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Chicago

Few cities hold as much heavy steel in motion as Chicago. Freight railroads converge here, so wheelsets, axles, couplers and bogie frames pass through overhaul shops, and fatigue cracking in those parts is exactly what magnetic particle testing is good at finding. The steel industry along the southern lakeshore, on both sides of the Illinois-Indiana line, relies on cranes that pour and move ladles, so hooks, trunnions, sheave pins and crane rail attachments are examined on a maintenance cycle. Refineries at Whiting, Joliet and Lemont bring pressure vessels, nozzles, skirts and tank shell attachments into scope, especially during turnarounds when equipment is open and the surface is clean.

Chicago's bridges add another class of work. The city's trunnion bascule leaves carry machinery, trunnion shafts and welded steel connections that live under repeated load, and steel bridges throughout the region need crack checks at repaired details. West of the city, Rockford-area shops make gears, shafts and landing-gear style components where grinding and heat-treatment cracks are the concern, and fabricators across the metro build structural steel and pressure parts that need in-process weld checks while rework is still easy.

  • Refinery vessel and piping welds, nozzle and support attachment welds, tank shell attachments
  • Mill and crane components: hooks, trunnions, couplings, roll necks, sheave pins
  • Rail and transit parts: axles, wheels, couplers, bogie and truck frames
  • Bridge and structural steel: fillet and groove welds, repaired details, lifting lugs

What MT detects, and what it cannot

Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. The inspector magnetizes the part, applies fine iron particles, and any discontinuity that interrupts the magnetic field pulls particles into a visible line. It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps and seams, and some flaws just under the surface. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys, which do not hold a useful field, and it does not see deep internal flaws.

Field direction matters. A crack shows best when it crosses the lines of magnetic flux at a right angle, so the code requires two examinations with the field turned roughly ninety degrees between them. A single pass can miss a crack that happens to run parallel to the field. Surface condition matters too: heavy scale, weld spatter and thick coatings reduce sensitivity, and the part has to be dry and free of oil. Where MT does not apply, penetrant testing handles non-magnetic metals and ultrasonic testing handles internal and wall-loss questions.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply in Chicago

The technique comes from ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E709 as a guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance is set by the construction or repair code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 covers vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 covers process piping, and AWS D1.1 covers structural steel welds, with AWS D1.5 for state bridge work. In each case the numbers of acceptable indications and their size limits come from that code, not from the technician.

Illinois controls repairs to registered equipment through the National Board Inspection Code. A licensed repair organization files a repair or alteration form after the work, and used or relocated equipment needs a certificate inspection before it returns to service. Magnetic particle examination of the excavation and the finished weld is part of the record behind those forms. Inside the city limits the Chicago Department of Buildings Boiler Inspection Bureau, not the state, is the inspecting authority for boilers and unfired pressure vessels, so repair records are confirmed with the right office before work begins. For the state's own rules see the Office of the State Fire Marshal boiler and pressure vessel page, and for background on repairs see the National Board. A refinery owner also has process safety obligations under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), which expects mechanical integrity work to follow good engineering practice. Our explainer on Article 7 requirements sets out the technique rules in plain terms.

How the examination is performed

For field welds the usual tool is an electromagnetic yoke. An alternating-current yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician checks that lift before use with a standard weight. The yoke is placed across the weld, particles are applied while the field is on, and the area is examined; then the yoke is turned about ninety degrees and the pass is repeated. Prods are kept off finished pressure-retaining surfaces because an arc strike is itself a rejectable condition.

Where sensitivity matters, such as hydrogen-service vessels or fatigue-critical parts, wet fluorescent particles are used. These need a darkened viewing area and a UV-A lamp whose intensity is checked, and the particles are suspended in a carrier fluid whose concentration is measured. Visible dry powder is easier outdoors on rough welds. A field indicator or shim shows that the setup is giving a usable field. If residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining or a sensitive instrument, the part is demagnetized and checked afterward. Thin non-magnetic coatings can be examined through only up to the limit the procedure demonstrates; thicker paint means removal back to metal or a qualification on a coated piece, and that choice should be agreed before the crew arrives.

Common MT findings and what happens next

On Chicago structural and rail steel the usual finds are fatigue cracks starting at weld toes and sharp changes of section, crater cracks at the end of a pass, and lack-of-fusion openings that reach the surface along a fillet. On heat-treated shafts and gears the finds are grinding checks and quench cracks, which show as fine networks. Indications that are rounded and small are often non-relevant, caused by a change of section or a magnetic writing effect, and the technician re-examines them after light cleaning to decide whether they are real. A confirmed linear indication is marked, measured and reported, and the owner or engineer decides whether to grind it out, weld repair it or remove the part. Atlantis does not decide the repair; after a repair the same examination is repeated to prove the crack is gone, and that second report goes into the same file.

It helps to have the drawing, the weld map and the previous report on hand when the technician arrives. A known cracked location or a past repair tells the technician where to look hardest, and it lets the report say whether an indication is new or has changed since the last campaign.

Who performs the work

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the indications. The magnetic particle procedure is approved, and each report reviewed, by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Chicago. Crews are mobilized to your site with the yokes, lamps, particles and calibration items the procedure calls for, and we confirm the travel and orientation requirements at the quoting stage. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a customer specification requires a particular qualification beyond the written practice, tell us up front and we will say what is realistic.

What an MT report contains

The report names the component and its location, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its calibration or lift check, the particles and carrier, the surface condition, the lighting measurements for fluorescent work, and the technician and level. Each reportable indication is located and sized on a sketch, with a note on whether it relieved on re-examination after light grinding. The disposition states accept or reject against the code criteria you named. An ASNT Level III reviews it before issue. If your repair file needs a specific form or a photograph log, send the template with your inquiry so the report matches your record.

Planning an MT job in Chicago

Chicago climate is a real planning factor. Winter days can be far below freezing, and cold particles, cold carrier fluid and stiff hands all reduce sensitivity; the procedure should state the allowed surface temperature, and the crew may need to warm the work area or the part. Summer heat on a refinery structure can make hot surfaces unsafe for wet methods and calls for dry powder. Humidity and rain stop outdoor work. Plants in the Calumet region, the Joliet corridor and the steel district run badge and safety orientation processes, and turnaround schedules are fixed months ahead, so the useful time to call is during scoping. Rail yards need track protection and bridges need lane or waterway closures arranged by the owner. Tell us the realities of your site and we will build the schedule around them.

MT, PT or UT for your Chicago job

A short scoping call usually settles it. Tell us the material grade, the surface condition and what failure you are worried about, and we will say which method answers it, and whether a second method should be on the same visit to save a return trip to the site.

The material and the question decide it. On carbon steel welds where you want surface cracks, MT is fast and sensitive. On stainless, aluminum or alloy parts where MT cannot be used, choose penetrant testing in Chicago. When the question is remaining wall or a flaw below the surface, choose ultrasonic testing in Chicago. Our national magnetic particle testing page and the complete MT guide cover the service and the theory, and the MT versus PT comparison helps if you are deciding between the two on a mixed-material job.

Training your own MT technicians

If you want in-house capability, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the wider magnetic particle testing training page explains how the course and practical fit your written practice. Chicago employers can read about NDT training in Chicago, and statewide inspection coverage is on the Illinois inspection services page. For written practice work, see written practice development.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials such as carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not carry a usable magnetic field, so those parts need penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Do you have a lab or office in Chicago?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Chicago. Technicians are mobilized to your site with the yokes, lamps and particles the procedure needs, and we confirm travel and site orientation details when we quote.

faq.q: Why does the examination need two directions?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it crosses the magnetic field, so ASME Section V Article 7 requires two examinations with the field turned roughly ninety degrees between them. A single pass can miss a crack that runs parallel to the field.

faq.q: Can you inspect through paint?
faq.a: Only through a thin non-magnetic coating, and only up to the thickness the written procedure has demonstrated. Heavier paint has to be removed or the procedure qualified on a coated sample, which we agree before the crew mobilizes.

faq.q: When is wet fluorescent MT chosen over dry powder?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles under UV-A light are chosen when sensitivity matters, for example on hydrogen-service vessels or fatigue-critical parts. Visible dry powder suits rough outdoor welds where a darkened viewing area is impractical.

faq.q: Which code sets the acceptance criteria?
faq.a: The code that built or governs the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel or AWS D1.5 for bridges. The owner or engineer names it before the job.

faq.q: Is demagnetization included?
faq.a: It is done when residual magnetism could affect later welding, machining or sensitive equipment, and the report records it. Tell us if the part goes back into service or on to another process so we can plan it.

faq.q: Who approves the MT procedure and reviews the report?
faq.a: An ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews each report. Level II technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, perform the examination and interpret the indications.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Chicago, IL | PT Testing
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing of stainless, alloy and aluminum welds, castings and machined parts in Chicago, visible or fluorescent dye. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Chicago, Illinois
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes liquid penetrant technicians to Chicago-area plants, fabrication shops and rail facilities to find surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps in non-magnetic and machined parts. If magnetic particle testing cannot be used on your material, dye penetrant inspection usually can. Request a PT quote for your Chicago site with the material, the part list and the code, and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Chicago

Chicago's industrial base is wider than its steel reputation suggests, and much of it is stainless, aluminum and alloy work that magnetic methods cannot touch. Food, beverage and pharmaceutical producers in the metro area run stainless process piping, tanks and heat exchangers, and weld quality on those systems is checked with penetrant before commissioning. Refineries at Whiting, Joliet and Lemont have austenitic and alloy piping, weld overlay and cladding where surface cracking is a concern, and turnaround repairs on those materials call for dye penetrant on the excavation and the final pass.

Machine shops and foundries around the region supply gears, housings, valve bodies and castings that arrive in stainless, aluminum or bronze, and penetrant is the practical way to screen them for cracks and shrinkage openings. Rail and transit shops use PT on aluminum body repairs, stainless brake and piping components, and journal surfaces where the metal is not suitable for magnetic work. Boiler and pressure vessel repair firms use it on stainless nozzle welds and on the root and cap passes of alloy repairs.

  • Stainless and nickel-alloy piping welds, weld overlay, cladding and tube-to-tubesheet joints
  • Food, beverage and pharmaceutical stainless vessels and process lines
  • Machined parts, castings and forgings in non-magnetic alloys
  • Aluminum and stainless repairs on rail and transit equipment

What penetrant testing finds, and what it misses

Penetrant testing finds only flaws that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid is applied, it is drawn into any crack, pore or lap by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out to form a visible indication. That makes it a reliable surface method on any non-porous material, ferrous or not: stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, brass and even ceramics.

The limits are just as clear. A flaw that does not break the surface will not show, however large it is inside the metal. A smeared surface, for example from grinding, shot peening or machining that has closed the crack mouth, can hide a real crack, so surface preparation is part of the technique. Porous materials absorb penetrant and produce a bright background. Oil, paint, rust and weld spatter block the liquid from entering the flaw. For internal flaws or wall thickness, ultrasonic testing is the answer, and for cracks on carbon steel where speed matters, magnetic particle testing is often quicker.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT

The technique comes from ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the general-industry practice. Acceptance rules come from the construction or repair code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 sets them for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural welds. Under those codes a linear indication above the stated length, or a group of rounded indications above the stated count, is rejectable, and the technician reports what was found without deciding on the owner's behalf whether a repair is worth it.

Chicago work also touches Illinois pressure equipment rules. The Office of the State Fire Marshal runs the state boiler and pressure vessel program and the City of Chicago Department of Buildings runs its own Boiler Inspection Bureau for equipment inside the city limits, so repair records on a registered vessel go to the right authority. The state publishes its boiler and pressure vessel FAQs and the city explains its process on the Boiler Inspections page. For a read on Article 6 itself, see our explainer on Article 6 requirements. Under owner programs for refineries and chemical plants, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) expects inspection to follow recognized good engineering practice.

How the penetrant process is carried out

The sequence has fixed steps and each one is controlled. The surface is cleaned and dried, then the penetrant is applied and left to dwell for the time the procedure sets, which depends on the material, the flaw type and the temperature. Excess is removed by the method named in the procedure, whether water-washable, solvent-removable or post-emulsifiable, and a developer is applied in a thin even coat. After a development period the surface is examined, with visible-dye systems read under white light and fluorescent systems read in a darkened area under UV-A light.

Chemistry matters on stainless and nickel alloys. The procedure limits the sulfur and halogen content of the penetrant materials used on those alloys because residues can damage them, and the technician cleans the surface thoroughly afterward. A solvent-removable visible system is the common field choice because it needs no water supply or electric darkroom. Fluorescent penetrant is chosen when the acceptance class demands higher sensitivity, for example on critical machined parts. Every batch of material is checked against its certification, and the procedure states what is done if an indication needs to be re-examined.

Surface preparation and cleaning

Most failed penetrant examinations fail before the penetrant goes on. As-welded surfaces carry spatter, slag and oxide that cover real flaws, and machined or ground surfaces may have smeared metal over a crack. The procedure therefore sets how the surface is prepared: wire brushing or light grinding for weld areas, solvent cleaning to remove oil and grease, and in some cases an etch or a controlled mechanical method that reopens a smeared surface. The part is then dried completely, because water in a crack keeps the penetrant out. On Chicago jobs where the part has been painted or coated, the coating is removed in the examination area, and the owner or coating contractor needs to be scheduled around it.

After the examination the developer and penetrant residues are removed, which matters on stainless and nickel alloys going back into service and on any surface that will later be welded or coated. Where a part will be repaired, the technician marks the area, then repeats the full penetrant sequence on the repaired weld so the file shows both the original finding and the clean result.

Common PT findings and how they are reported

Indications fall into a few shapes. A continuous line usually points to a crack or a lap. A row of dots can be a line of pores or a tight crack seen through a rough surface. Scattered round marks are often porosity. In machined stainless and aluminum parts, a shrinkage opening in a casting looks like a rough cluster. Each is described by shape, location and size, and compared against the acceptance criteria, which usually limit linear indication length and the number of rounded indications in a stated area. Indications that could be false, for example from a surface irregularity or insufficient cleaning, are re-examined after cleaning rather than called as defects. The report separates what was relevant from what was not, so the owner reads a clear result.

Who does the work

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the process, applies the materials, interprets the indications and reports them. Penetrant procedures are written to the code and approved by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, who also reviews each report. Atlantis has no office in Chicago, and the crew is mobilized to your site with the materials, lamps and cleaning supplies the procedure calls for. We confirm travel and orientation requirements when we quote. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Customer-specific qualification requirements should be flagged at the start so we can say what is practical.

What a PT report contains

A penetrant report names the part and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by brand and batch, the dwell and development times, the surface temperature, the lighting level for visible or fluorescent work, and the technician and level. Each indication is located and sized, with a sketch or photo where useful, and the result is an accept or reject call against the criteria you named. An ASNT Level III reviews the report before it is issued. For a repair file, say whether you need before-and-after records so we can match the sequence of the work.

Planning a PT job in Chicago

Penetrant is the method most affected by temperature, and Chicago weather makes that a planning item. The standard procedure under Article 6 covers a part and materials temperature of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside that range the procedure has to be qualified for the actual temperature. Winter mornings on an outdoor repair are often below the range, so the crew may need heating, enclosures or a qualified low-temperature procedure, and summer sun can push steel above the upper limit. Rain and humidity delay drying and development. Plants in the Calumet region and Joliet corridor use badge and orientation steps, and refinery turnarounds are scheduled well ahead of time, so contact us while scoping. Food and pharmaceutical sites add their own gowning, cleaning and residue rules, which we need to know before the penetrant materials are chosen.

PT, MT or UT for your Chicago job

A short scoping call usually settles it. Tell us the alloy, the surface finish and the failure mode you are worried about, and we will say whether penetrant answers it or whether another method should be added to the same visit to avoid a second trip to the site.

Choose penetrant when the material is not ferromagnetic or the part is machined, or when you want one method that works on every material in the scope. Choose magnetic particle testing in Chicago for carbon and low-alloy steel where speed and sensitivity to fine cracks matter. Choose ultrasonic testing in Chicago for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. The national penetrant testing page describes the service in general terms, and the MT versus PT comparison is useful for mixed-material scopes.

Training your own penetrant technicians

PT is among the quickest methods to bring in house. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and the general penetrant testing training page shows how the course and practical examination fit your written practice. Trainees can practice on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator. Chicago employers can read about NDT training in Chicago, and statewide coverage is on the Illinois inspection services page. For a written practice, see written practice development.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: Only flaws that are open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, pores and seams, on non-porous materials. It cannot find a flaw sealed inside the metal, so internal questions need ultrasonic testing instead.

faq.q: When should I use PT instead of magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Use penetrant on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic metals, and on machined parts where you want one method for every material. Magnetic particle testing is usually quicker on carbon steel.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Chicago?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Chicago. Technicians are mobilized to your site with the materials, lamps and cleaning supplies the procedure calls for, and travel and orientation steps are confirmed in the quote.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant work?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 covers 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters on Chicago winter outdoor jobs.

faq.q: Visible dye or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye is the common field choice because it needs only white light. Fluorescent penetrant gives higher sensitivity and is used where the acceptance class requires it, in a darkened area under UV-A light.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Grinding, peening or machining can smear metal over a crack and close its mouth, and oil or paint blocks the liquid. The procedure specifies cleaning, and sometimes etching, so the surface is truly open before penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Is penetrant safe on stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes, when the materials are the low sulfur and low halogen types the procedure requires and the surface is cleaned afterward. We record the product batches in the report so the control can be shown later.

faq.q: Which code governs acceptance?
faq.a: The construction or repair code for your item, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. The owner or engineer names it before the job, and the report cites the criteria used.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Chicago, IL: UT and RT Review
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. For Chicago welds, ask about UT or Level III radiograph review. Request a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Chicago: What Atlantis Offers Instead
rt.html:
Atlantis does not carry out radiographic testing anywhere in the United States. If you searched for radiography in Chicago, this page explains why, and what we can do for a weld or casting scope: ultrasonic examination where your code allows it, and independent ASNT Level III review of radiographs made by a licensed contractor. Tell us about the Chicago scope and we reply within one business day.

Why Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States

Industrial radiography uses sealed gamma sources or X-ray equipment, and in the United States it is a licensed activity. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission sets the rules in 10 CFR Part 34, and Agreement States such as Illinois run equivalent programs; in Illinois the Illinois Emergency Management Agency licenses radioactive materials. A company needs the license, trained and certified radiographers, source security and exposure-control procedures before it can legally expose a weld. Atlantis does not offer that service here and does not claim to. We would rather say so plainly than let a Chicago buyer assume otherwise.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative in Chicago

For many weld scopes the question behind a radiography request is whether the weld has internal flaws. Ultrasonic testing answers it without a radiation exclusion zone, which is attractive in occupied Chicago plants and at busy refineries where clearing an area for exposure stops other trades. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own acceptance criteria for groove welds examined by UT, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 permits UT in place of radiography only under specific conditions.

That substitution is not ours to decide alone. It has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer of record and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job, and recorded in the examination plan. When it is agreed, ultrasonic testing in Chicago from Atlantis covers shear-wave weld examination to a written procedure, with the reference level and indication log in the report. Other Chicago scopes may be better served by magnetic particle or penetrant surface examination.

ASNT Level III radiography review without a radiation license

Reviewing an image does not involve a source, so it needs no radiation license. The review service covers an independent read of radiographs, film or digital, and their technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. It includes a second read on disputed indications, a check of image quality indicators and density or contrast against the requirement, and review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. The review is carried out under the direction of Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Images stay with the contractor who made them; we review what you send and report our findings to you.

This is useful on Chicago projects where an owner or general contractor wants a second pair of expert eyes on radiography they did not witness, or where an acceptance decision is contested. It does not replace the contractor's own Level II interpretation. For help setting expectations with a radiography subcontractor, see outsourced Level III consulting.

Radiography training and your written practice

If your Chicago team needs to understand radiography, Atlantis teaches the theory side through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Radiographic work on real sources still requires a licensed program run by the employer. We can also help you write or review the radiography portion of your SNT-TC-1A written practice, which is covered under written practice development. Chicago employers can read about NDT training in Chicago, and statewide inspection services are on the Illinois inspection services page.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Chicago?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing anywhere in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules and Agreement State programs such as the one in Illinois. Ultrasonic testing and Level III radiograph review are available from Atlantis instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows UT in place of RT under specific conditions. The substitution must be agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can you review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III reviews film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and gives a second read on disputed indications. The images stay with the contractor.

faq.q: Do you recommend a radiography contractor in Chicago?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. We can review the contractor procedure and the images afterward, so your acceptance decision rests on an independent technical opinion.

faq.q: Where can my team learn radiography theory?
faq.a: A radiographic testing Level 2 course covering theory is available from Atlantis. Practical work with sources must be done under a licensed program, and your written practice under SNT-TC-1A defines who is qualified in your company.
